1.note: The word translated as **bending forward** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have copied a similar-looking original consonant wrong, resulting in this word. With that consonant, it would say “marching,” which seems to fit the meaning of this passage better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [marching]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **greatness** and **strength**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [because he is very strong]
This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [righteously]

2.note: The speaker is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [is your clothing red and why are your garments red]

The point of this comparison is that just as **one treading in a wine press** has his clothing stained red by the grape juice, so **your clothing** is red. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [stained red as if you had been treading grapes in a wine press]

3.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if he had **trodden a winepress** when he punished the nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have punished the nations, crushing them like grapes in a winepress, by myself]
See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Because I was very angry, I trampled them]

Yahweh is using **in my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in my anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in my anger]

Yahweh is using **in my heat** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in my fury.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in my fury] or [in my wrath]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [and their blood splattered all over my clothing and stained everything I was wearing]

3.q: וְ⁠יֵ֤ז נִצְחָ⁠ם֙ עַל בְּגָדַ֔⁠י וְ⁠כָל מַלְבּוּשַׁ֖⁠י אֶגְאָֽלְתִּי
3.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the blood of the peoples he destroyed were the **juice** of grapes crushed in a winepress. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their blood spattered on my garments, and I stained all of my clothing]

4.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the day when I would avenge myself]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the day of vengeance were an object that had been **in my heart**. He means that he had determined to carry it out. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was something I had determined to carry out]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **year** that is characterized by **my redeemed ones**, that is, the year in which he would redeem his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the year for me to redeem my people]

5.note: Here, **my arm** represents Yahweh’s own strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [So my own strength saved for me]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **it** separately, even though the verb translated as **it supported me** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was his own wrath, and not anyone else, that supported him when he found no other helper. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [my anger itself supported me]

6.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if he **made them drunk**. He means that he made them stagger helplessly under his judgment. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I made them stagger and fall to the ground]

Here, **their blood** represents their lifeblood. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I sent their lifeblood into the soil]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulnesses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how faithful Yahweh has been to his covenant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and how very good he has been]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the people descended from Israel were a **house**, that is, a single household or family. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the nation descended from Israel]

Isaiah refers to the people of Israel first as **us** and then as **them**, even though he belongs to that same group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the same person to refer to them in both places. Alternate translation: [has rewarded us … he has rewarded us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because he is compassionate]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and because he very faithfully keeps his covenant with them]

8.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Israel were his **sons**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [children who will not deal falsely]

9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **affliction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [In all the times they were afflicted]

The phrase **he was not afflicted** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [affliction was to him]

Here, **his face** represents Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the angel of his presence]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **love** and **mercy**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [Because he loved them and had compassion on them]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh cared for his people the way a parent **lifted them up and carried them**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he supported and sustained them]

Isaiah is using **all of the days of eternity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “long ago” or “throughout ancient times.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [throughout ancient times]

10.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his Spirit, who is holy]

Isaiah is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **rebelled** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between what Yahweh had done for his people, as described in the previous verses, and how the people responded. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But they were the ones who rebelled]

Isaiah is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **fought** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh himself became the one fighting against his own people as their enemy. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he himself fought with them]

11.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the days of long ago, the days of Moses]

This is the beginning of what the people said. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a first-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a first-level quotation.

11.q: אַיֵּ֣ה הַֽ⁠מַּעֲלֵ֣⁠ם מִ⁠יָּ֗ם אֵ֚ת רֹעֵ֣י צֹאנ֔⁠וֹ
11.note: The people are using the question form to express their longing for Yahweh to help them as he did in the past. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [How we long for the one who brought them up from the sea with our leaders!]

The implication is that this refers to the Sea of Reeds, which Yahweh divided when he brought the Israelites out of Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [out of the Sea of Reeds]

Here the people are speaking as if the leaders whom Yahweh set over Israel were **shepherds** and the people themselves were his **flock**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the leaders of his people]

12.note: The people are using the possessive form to describe an **arm**, his power, that is characterized by **splendor**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his splendid power]

Here, **the right hand of Moses** represents the place of honor and power at Moses’ side. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to a place of honor at Moses’ side]
Here, **their faces** represents “in front of them.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of them]

Here, **name** represents Yahweh’s reputation or fame. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [an eternal reputation for himself]

13.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a horse in the wilderness** does not stumble, so the people **did not stumble** as Yahweh led them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as a horse does not stumble in the wilderness]

Isaiah is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [they walked very securely]

14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **cattle going down into a valley** find a place of rest, so **the Spirit of Yahweh made him rest**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as cattle going down into a valley find a place of rest]

The pronoun **him** refers to the people of Israel, spoken of here as a single group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Spirit of Yahweh made the people of Israel rest]

Here the people begin to address Yahweh directly in the second person as **you**, even though they have been speaking about him in the third person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could refer to Yahweh in the same person throughout this passage. Alternate translation: [Thus he led his people, to make for himself a name of splendor]

15.note: The word translated as **Look** is an imperative, but the people are using it to make a request rather than to give a command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a request. Alternate translation: [Please look from the heavens and see]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **holiness** and **splendor**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [from where you dwell, holy and splendid]

The people are using the question form to express their distress that Yahweh no longer seems to act powerfully on their behalf. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We no longer see your zeal and your mighty deeds!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **zeal**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [are your zealous actions]

Here, **your inner parts** represents Yahweh’s deep feelings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The stirring of your deep feelings]

16.note: Here the people are speaking as if Yahweh were their **father**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are the one who created us]

The implication is that **Israel** here refers to Jacob, the ancestor of the nation, who is long dead and so does not know his descendants now. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and Jacob our ancestor does not recognize us]

17.note: The people are using the question form to express their complaint, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not make us wander, Yahweh, from your ways!]

Here the people are speaking as if the way Yahweh wants them to live were **ways** or paths that a person walks along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from how you want us to live]

Here the people are speaking as if making them stubborn were causing their **heart** to become hard. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do you make us stubbornly turn]

The word translated as **Return** is an imperative, but the people are using it to make a plea rather than to give a command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a request. Alternate translation: [Please return]

Here the people are speaking as if they were an **inheritance** that Yahweh had received. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the tribes that are your possession]

18.note: The people are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For a little while]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your holy people]

19.note: The expression **was not called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you never called your name over them]

The people are using **your name was not called over them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they did not belong to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were not yours]
